processing: A baked or part pan-fired, part baked green tea, worked gently to keep each bud and its leaves joined. The orchid note is natural, not from scenting with flowers.
harvest_season: Spring. As with other Dabie Mountain greens, the early pickings are the most prized.
appearance_dry: Bud and leaves joined like a sprig of orchid grass, finely curled and slightly hooked, in even emerald green.
appearance_wet: Buds and leaves stay joined and stand up as they open in the glass.
taste_profile: Fresh, brisk and sweetly mellow, with a quiet orchid fragrance that rises with the steam.

brewing.notes: Use a glass: watching the sprigs stand up is half of it. Cooler water keeps the orchid note from getting lost.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring's harvest, as with other Anhui greens, and best drunk within about a year; earlier pickings cost more. Production is scattered and much of it is sold by the farmers themselves, so quality varies more than the name suggests.
description:
Shucheng Xiaolanhua, little orchid of Shucheng, comes from the southeastern foot of the Dabie Mountains in Anhui. The orchid is in the look and the aroma, and neither comes from flowers: the bud and leaves stay joined like a sprig of orchid grass, and the fragrance comes from the plant and the place.

It is a baked or part-baked green, handled so that each sprig stays whole. Local judges talk about three orchids: orchid shape, orchid-grass colour and orchid scent.

In a glass the sprigs stand upright and open slowly, and the fragrance is often described as a line of scent rising with the steam. The cup is tender green, fresh and sweetly mellow. Most people lose it by using water that is too hot.

Buy the latest spring and ask who made it, because much of this tea is made and sold by individual farmers. If you enjoy it, try Yuexi Cuilan next, a modern tea built on the same little orchid tradition.
history:
Sources date it to the late Ming and early Qing, and one account says orchid tea was made around the border of Shucheng and Lujiang before then. Like several county teas of Anhui, it is said to have been sent as tribute in its day.

In 2015 it received national protection as a geographical indication. Its traditional craft was also the starting point for Yuexi Cuilan, created in the neighbouring county in the 1980s.
